replying_to: Replying to Can Mamba Learn In Context with Outliers? A Theoretical Generalization Analysis
display_title: Official Review of Submission7901 by Reviewer 2qkh

summary.value: This paper provides a theoretical study of in-context learning (ICL) capabilities, focusing on a one-layer Mamba model, which consists of linear attention plus a non-linear gating layer. Focusing on synthetic binary classification prompts with additive outliers, the authors prove convergence and sample-complexity guarantees, and provide conditions under which the model generalizes to unseen tasks, and remains robust to distribution-shifted outliers. Mainly, the bound permits a test outlier fraction value that is more flexible than a linear Transformer, capped at 1/2, which the authors attribute to the nonlinear gating layer that suppresses corrupted examples, and emphasizes pattern-matching entries. Empirical demonstrations illustrate the main theorems.

strengths.value:
- Clear theoretical results and comparison with Mamba vs. Linear Transformer. This strengthens the paper's analysis that gating helps in ignoring noisy examples.
- The theoretical results match the synthetic experiments, such as Mamba's tolerance to many outliers, and sensitivity to outliers near the query.
- More specifically, the paper includes the analysis of comparative training bounds and robustness regime.
- The synthetic generation setup is fully specified (i.e. the parameters) and the paper discusses the limitations in conclusions.

weaknesses.value:
The weaknesses I will address are intertwined with questions that I have regarding this work. 
- Since the paper points out the limitation of single-head linear attention Transformer, i.e. the tolerance parameter alpha having to be less than 1/2, a brief discussion, even if not supported by theoretical results, on whether more realistic Transformers would suffer less from this constraint. In other words, would having multiple heads help mitigate this issue?
- The manuscript will be much easier to read and understand if takeaway messages for each figure are listed in the captions.

questions.value:
- It seems form Table 1 that closest to query (CQ) hurts Mamba's performance substantially. I think this result intuitively makes sense if we take the RNN perspective of understanding Mamba, which could mean that while gating layers can suppress outliers, it needs to see sufficient number of examples before being able to do so. In this regard, (i) what could be a possible mitigation strategy to this? (ii) This also could suggest that Mamba is strongly biased against the first few samples that it has seen, learns the underlying function, and uses that for the rest of the in-context examples. First, I would like to double check with the authors if my understanding is correct. If it is, I am wondering if this could be a reason that Mamba performs better when alpha is larger than 1/2, and even closer to 1. 
- In the regard of the first question, it would be interesting to see what the number 78% for the Linear Transformer means. Is it trying to do fit a least squares function with the presence of noise? If such functions exist, does that match the empirical performance of 78% we are seeing, regardless of the positions of the queries?

I believe the paper is solid, but there could be much more interesting discussions that can happen around these results. I would be inclined to raise the score if we see some of them during the rebuttal.

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable evaluation and suggestions.

**W1: Since the paper ... a brief discussion on whether more realistic Transformers would suffer less from this constraint. In other words, would having multiple heads help mitigate this issue?**

**A1**: This is a great question. Regarding whether realistic Transformers are less constrained by the $\alpha<1/2$ condition, we have conducted experiments using multi-head linear Transformers and softmax attention. The simple conclusion is that increasing the number of heads does not provide noticeable benefits for our task, which lacks causal relationships between tokens. When switching to softmax attention, the $\alpha<1/2$ restriction is significantly alleviated, and robustness improves. 

First, we experiment on linear Transformers with the number of heads ranging from 1 to 4. We enlarge the dimension from $24$ to $72$, so that the divided dimension on each head is not smaller than the number of features. Other settings are kept as the same in our submission, where the fractions of outlier examples in training and testing are $p\_a=0.4$, and $\alpha=0.5$, respectively. The results are summarized as follows, where $H$ denotes the number of heads. Recall that FQ, R, CQ represent three kinds of outlier placements, i.e., "farthest from the query", "random positions", and "closest to the query", respectively.

| |$H=1$|$H=2$|$H=3$|$H=4$|
|--|--|--|--|--|
|FQ|93.68%|93.90%|92.86%|91.54%|
|R|94.12%|95.08%|93.10%|90.90%|
|CQ|93.96%|94.18%|92.74%|90.86%|

Our results show that increasing the number of heads to $H=2$ slightly improves the performance of the linear Transformer, but $H=3, 4$ degrade the performance. We conjecture that the effectiveness of multi-head attention varies, depending on the level of causal relationship within tokens [Chen et al., 2024b], while we do not explicitly model causal relationships in the experiments. 

Second, we also evaluated the performance of softmax attention under different values of $\alpha$ and different outlier placements. We show the results of three-layer single-head softmax Transformers and linear Transformers when $\alpha=0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8$ in the following table. We can observe that, compared with the linear Transformer, the softmax Transformer avoids the sharp drop in test accuracy that occurs for linear Transformers when $\alpha>1/2$.
|Softmax Transformer|$\alpha=0.4$|$\alpha=0.5$|$\alpha=0.6$|$\alpha=0.7$|$\alpha=0.8$|
|--|--|--|--|--|--|
|FQ|99.60%|99.40%|99.14%|98.40%|94.80%|
|R|99.63%|99.26%|99.02%|98.04%|95.58%|
|CQ|99.60%|99.38%|99.12%|98.24%|95.22%|

|Linear Transformer|$\alpha=0.4$|$\alpha=0.5$|$\alpha=0.6$|$\alpha=0.7$|$\alpha=0.8$|
|--|--|--|--|--|--|
|FQ|96.54%|93.68%|89.68%|81.18%|69.10%|
|R|96.48%|94.12%|90.66%|81.00%|67.78%|
|CQ|96.30%|93.96%|90.08%|80.82%|68.70%|

We then compare the results of three-layer single-head softmax Transformer, linear Transformer, and mamba models when $\alpha=0.5$. When $\alpha=0.5$ is fixed, the performance of softmax attention under the FQ and R outlier placements is close to that of Mamba. Moreover, unlike Mamba, which exhibits a significant accuracy drop in the CQ setting, the softmax Transformer still maintains high accuracy in this case. This is also consistent with [Wang et al., 2024], which shows that without robustness training, Mamba is more vulnerable than the softmax Transformer to outliers that appear near the query, leading to a substantial decrease in performance [Wang et al., 2025]. The reason why we only theoretically study linear Transformers is that we would like to highlight the effect of nonlinear gating of Mamba by a fair comparison. This is discussed in the updated Remark 6. 

| |Softmax Transformer|LT|Mamba|
|--|--|--|--|
|FQ|99.40%|93.68%|99.73%|
|R|99.26%|94.12%|99.67%|
|CQ|99.38%|93.96%|82.73%|

We have incorporated the above discussion in the updated version. 

Wang et al., 2025. Understanding and Mitigating Bottlenecks of State Space Models through the Lens of Recency and Over-smoothing. At ICLR.

**W2: The manuscript will be much easier to read and understand if takeaway messages for each figure are listed in the captions.**

**A2**: Thank you for the suggestion. We have revised the captions of Figures 2-5 accordingly in the updated version. Specifically, in Figure 2, we add "Trained Mamba models can tolerate more than $1/2$ fraction of outlier examples, while linear Transformers cannot." In Figure 3, we add "The summation of 1st-layer attention scores on examples with the same relevant pattern as the query is much larger than that with a different relevant pattern from the query." In Figure 4, we add "The 1st-layer gating values of examples with (red) additive outliers are small, while examples without (green) additive outliers are large and decay exponentially. " In Figure 5, we add "Mamba performs better than linear Transformers if outliers are FQ or R, but exhibits a significant performance drop in the CQ setting."

comment.value:
**Q1: It seems form Table 1 that closest to query (CQ) hurts Mamba's performance substantially…… In this regard, (i) what could be a possible mitigation strategy to this? (ii) This also could suggest that Mamba is strongly biased against the first few samples that it has seen, learns the underlying function, and uses that for the rest of the in-context examples. First, I would like to double check with the authors if my understanding is correct. If it is, I am wondering if this could be a reason that Mamba performs better when alpha is larger than 1/2, and even closer to 1.**

A3: These are great questions and insightful interpretations. The understanding that Mamba is biased by the first few examples close to the query is partially correct, but this only applies to examples without outliers. In other words, two factors in Mamba are effective together: detecting outliers and then concentrating on the first few examples without outliers.   This is discussed in our Corollary 2 (ii). Specifically, Equation 18 quantitatively shows that the nonlinear gating value on examples without outliers decays exponentially as their distance from the query increases. As a result, the final ICL prediction depends on the functions associated with the examples closest to the query and on the predictions they produce. Because Mamba always prefers to select outlier-free examples for ICL prediction as demonstrated in Corollary 2(i), having an $\alpha>1/2$, i.e., more than half of the examples contain outliers, will not negatively affect the prediction. Linear attention cannot learn outliers and therefore cannot handle prediction when $\alpha>1/2$. 

Our Mamba results in Table 1 show that placing the outlier closest to the query is the most effective way to disrupt the ICL prediction of Mamba, especially when the test prompt contains a higher proportion of outliers than the training prompt. Regarding your first question, possible mitigation strategies for CQ, we believe one potential approach is to strengthen robust training so that the model becomes better at discarding examples containing outliers. For instance, we conduct an experiment by incorporating the CQ data in the training. Specifically, to avoid the training difficulty if all data are CQ, we use a simple strategy, i.e., we first train on data where outliers appear at random positions, and in the second half of training, we switch all data to the CQ data. With all other settings be the same, the ICL accuracies of FQ, R, and CQ are $98.00\\%$, $98.25\\%$, and $95.45\\%$, indicating that the poor performance of CQ is mitigated. 

We already include some of the discussion above in the Appendix B.1 and thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion.


**Q2: In the regard of the first question, it would be interesting to see what the number 78% for the Linear Transformer means. Is it trying to do fit a least squares function with the presence of noise? If such functions exist, does that match the empirical performance of 78% we are seeing, regardless of the positions of the queries?**

**A4**: A very sharp observation! Yes, some existing theoretical works on one-layer, single-head linear attention indeed show that the model implicitly fits the least-squares estimator in ICL. In our setting, the linear attention model can indeed fit such a function. Moreover, since the linear attention in our setting cannot learn the outlier, the ICL accuracy depends only on how many examples in the prompt contain outliers and lead to incorrect predictions, and is independent of the placements of those outlier examples. This also explains why, in Table 1, the ICL accuracies of linear attention are almost the same for all three outlier placements FQ, R, and CQ.
We tested the cases $\alpha = 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7$. The results show that, for a fixed $\alpha$, the ICL accuracy is similar across the three outlier placements FQ, R, and CQ. As $\alpha$ increases, the ICL accuracy degrades.

|Linear Transformer| $\alpha=0.4$| $\alpha=0.5$ | $\alpha=0.6$ | $\alpha=0.7$ | $\alpha=0.8$|
|--|--|--|--|--|--|
|FQ|96.54%|93.68%|89.68%|81.18%|69.10%|
|R|96.48%|94.12%|90.66%|81.00%|67.78%|
|CQ|96.30%|93.96%|90.08%|80.82%|68.70%|

Note that compared with the original version, we have modified the dimension and addressed several other issues, so the accuracies for the case $\alpha=0.5$ is updated. The conclusion remains the same, i.e., the accuracies for the three outlier placements are similar and are significantly lower than Mamba’s accuracies under the FQ and R placements. We already include the discussion above in the paper and thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestion.

summary.value:
This paper presents the first theoretical analysis of in-context learning (ICL) in Mamba. Specifically, the authors study a one-layer Mamba with a linear attention component followed by a nonlinear gating mechanism and analyze its ability to perform ICL on binary classification tasks—even when prompts contain additive outliers.
The paper’s main contributions are:
1. It provides quantitative convergence and generalization guarantees for Mamba trained on prompts with outliers, showing robustness even when nearly all examples are corrupted.
2. It theoretically compares Mamba to linear Transformers, proving that Mamba can generalize in the presence of a higher fraction of outliers.
3. It characterizes the mechanistic role of Mamba’s components: linear attention selects examples sharing relevant patterns with the query, while the gating mechanism suppresses outliers and emphasizes nearby examples.

Synthetic experiments support the theory by showing that Mamba achieves lower classification error than linear Transformers under various outlier corruption schemes.

strengths.value:
Originality:
This work is among the first to give a theoretical treatment of Mamba’s ICL mechanism, especially under the presence of outliers. Previous ICL analyses primarily focus on Transformers. The extension to Mamba—given its nonlinear gating and state-space formulation—is novel and nontrivial.

Technical quality:
The paper presents well-structured theorems (Theorems 1–4) detailing convergence, sample complexity, and robustness. The proofs seem grounded in prior analytical frameworks for Transformers (Li et al., 2024a,b) but adapted to handle the additional nonlinearity of gating. The comparison to linear Transformers provides useful insights into the tradeoff between convergence speed and robustness.

Significance:
Understanding Mamba’s ICL properties is highly relevant as Mamba-based models gain traction as efficient alternatives to Transformers. The result that Mamba tolerates a higher fraction of outliers could motivate more robust sequence modeling approaches in practice.

Clarity and organization:
The paper is generally well-written and logically organized.

weaknesses.value:
1. The task and outlier definition seem not natural and general. This limits the generality of the conclusions. It is unclear whether similar robustness properties would hold for more natural data distributions or real-world text prompts.

2. Several theorems introduce numerous symbols without sufficient intuitive explanation, which makes the results hard to interpret. The meaning of constants such as Θ(·), poly(·), and ranges should be contextualized more clearly.

3. The experiments are purely synthetic and cover only a very limited case. While they match the theory, they provide no evidence that these findings generalize to realistic NLP or vision tasks.

4. Recent empirical work shows that large Transformers can also exhibit robustness to mislabeling or outlier examples in ICL regimes. A discussion or comparison to this line of work is missing.

5. The analysis assumes that “examples close to the query” are beneficial, but if these nearby examples are adversarial or have opposite labels, the gating mechanism could amplify errors instead of mitigating them. This edge case should be acknowledged.

questions.value: How would the gating mechanism behave if the nearest examples to the query are misleading or adversarially labeled? Does the exponential decay still guarantee robustness, or could it amplify incorrect patterns?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable evaluation and suggestions.

**W1: The task and outlier definition seem not natural and general. This limits the generality of the conclusions. It is unclear whether similar robustness properties would hold for more natural data distributions or real-world text prompts.**

**A1**: Great question! First, the data formulation of relevant and irrelevant patterns that are orthogonal is inspired by the latent sparse representation of real-world data [Wright et al., 2010]. Specifically, the formulation of relevant patterns that determine labels is inspired by the observation that real-world data often admits a sparse representation [Wright et al., 2010], i.e., the data can be expressed using a set of low-dimensional and sparse patterns that form a dictionary, and the associated labels are functions of these underlying representations. Irrelevant patterns refer to additional information in the data that is unrelated to the classification task, e.g., backgrounds in images or unimportant words in language. Learning deep neural network features using a sparse representation formulation has been shown to be highly effective by strong empirical performance in diverse tasks such as face recognition and image denoising [Wright et al., 2010]. This indicates that sparse representation aligns well with the underlying structure of real-world data. Moreover, some other existing empirical works [Engler et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024] demonstrate that embeddings of real-world data between semantically different data are discriminative, which is also aligned with our data formulation based on relevant and irrelevant patterns. 

Second, the notion of additive outliers is motivated by data poisoning attacks, where the predicted label of a context example can be changed by inserting specific phrases into the context input. This is illustrated in Example 1 of our paper. Since an outlier is a phrase inserted into the sentence, we treat it as a new embedding added to the sentence embedding. Because such inserted phrases are typically unrelated to the task-specific keywords, for example, in Example 1, “James Bond” is unrelated to the keywords of sentiment classification, we accordingly assume that the embedding of the outlier is orthogonal to the relevant patterns. A similar assumption is also made in [Li et al., 2025] for robustness analysis of Transformers in ICL.

To address your concerns, we conduct two experiments to validate our data formulation and conclusion with a real-world setting. The dataset we use is the sentiment classification dataset SST-2.  We conduct Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on sentence vectors of different classes obtained by DistillBert. Then the classification task is performed on the data that only keeps a few PCA components. The following table shows that when keeping the top few principal components, i.e., 10 out of 768 in total, the classification performance using these principal components is already close to the baseline using original data. This indicates that real-world data can be represented as a linear combination of orthogonal vectors, where these principal components exactly correspond to relevant patterns we formulate. 

|# of principal components|5|7|10|768 (Baseline)|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Accuracy|74.08%|76.72%|78.90%|80.05%|



We then conduct an ICL experiment by constructing each prompt with 8 examples and one query. The outlier phrase “James Bond” is inserted into a randomly selected example at a random position. The training outlier fraction $p_a=0.25$. All models are constrained to have 3 layers and 2 heads. The linear Transformer models use linear attention. The table below compares Mamba and the linear Transformer under the testing outlier fraction $\alpha=0.75$ across the three outlier placements. Recall that FQ, R, CQ represent three kinds of outlier placements, i.e, “farthest from the query”, “random positions”, and “closest to the query”, respectively. The results show that Mamba performs better overall than the linear Transformer, and its performance at the CQ position is the lowest compared to FQ and R. This is consistent with the synthetic experiments in Table 1 of our paper and validates our analysis in Corollary 2 regarding the mechanism of nonlinear gating. We have included these results in Appendix B.2 of the updated paper.


||Mamba|LT|
|---|---|---|
|FQ|74.10%|70.18%|
|R|73.86%|69.98%|
|CQ|72.45%|69.82%|




Wright et al., 2010. Sparse representation for computer vision and pattern recognition. At Proceedings of IEEE.

Engler et al., 2022. SensePOLAR: Word sense aware interpretability for pre-trained contextual word embeddings. At EMNLP findings.

Liu et al., 2024. In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering. At ICML.

Li et al., 2025. On the Robustness of Transformers against Context Hijacking for Linear Classification. At Neurips.

comment.value:
**W2: Several theorems introduce numerous symbols without sufficient intuitive explanation. The meaning of constants such as $\Theta(·)$, $poly(·)$, and ranges should be contextualized more clearly.**

**A2**: Thank you for this question. In our initial submission, we have included the definition of numerous symbols in Table 2, and we put Table 2 in Appendix C due to the page limit. Specifically, the definition of $\Theta(\cdot)$ is that, if $f(x)=\Theta(g(x))$, then there exists $C>c>0$, $a>0$, such that $cg(x)\leq f(x)\leq Cg(x)$ for all $x>a$, which means that $f(x)$ increases in the order of $g(x)$. The definition of $\mathrm{poly}(\cdot)$ is that, if $f(x)=\mathrm{poly}(x)$, then there exists $k>0$ and a set of constants $\\{c_i\\}\_{i=0}\^k$, such that $f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^k c_i x^i$, which means $f(x)$ is a polynomial function of $x$ with a finite maximal power. $i\in [k]$ means that $i\in \\{j\in \mathbb{N}: 1\leq j\leq k\\}$. $(a,b)=\\{x: a<x<b\\}$, $[a,b)=\\{x: a\leq x<b\\}$, $(a,b]=\\{x: a<x\leq b\\}$, $[a,b]=\\{x: a\leq x\leq b\\}$. We have updated our Table 2 accordingly, following your suggestion. 

**W3: The experiments are purely synthetic and cover only a very limited case. While they match the theory, they provide no evidence that these findings generalize to realistic NLP or vision tasks.**

**A3**: Thank you to the reviewer for this question. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we conducted real-world ICL experiments. Please see A1 for the details. We have included this result in Appendix B.2 of the updated paper.

**W4: Recent empirical work shows that large Transformers can also exhibit robustness to mislabeling or outlier examples in ICL regimes. A discussion or comparison to this line of work is missing.**

**A4**: This is a very good question. Large Transformer models can achieve robustness to mislabeled or outlier examples in the ICL setting through appropriate white-box or black-box defense strategies. For instance, during instruction tuning, one can filter out outlier data or use early stopping to reduce the learning of outliers [Wan et al., 2023]. During ICL, outlier examples can be detected using perplexity-based criteria or grammar checks, or removed by rewriting the text [He et al., 2024]. These works indicate that, given sufficient expressive power, a properly trained Transformer model can also exhibit strong robustness with an appropriate prompt.

Regarding our analysis of Transformer robustness, we would like to clarify the following. First, our theoretical result states that under the one-layer single-head setting, after training on prompts with the same distribution containing outliers, Mamba is more robust than the linear Transformer. This result does not imply that Transformer models themselves cannot obtain good robustness. Our theoretical analysis is meant to highlight the additional advantage of Mamba’s nonlinear gating structure in detecting and removing outliers. Second, our theoretical conclusions apply to the linear Transformer rather than to all general Transformer models, like those with softmax attention. This restriction is imposed to avoid confounding effects from softmax attention, which would otherwise make it difficult to isolate the impact of nonlinear gating.

We have incorporated these into our revised manuscript. Specifically, we mention "one-layer" in P2 of Section 3.1 and the title of Section 3.4. We have added Remark 6 to emphasize that our work does not claim that Transformer models lack robustness. Rather, the analysis is intended solely to highlight the role of the nonlinear gating mechanism.

Wan et al., 2023. Poisoning Language Models During Instruction Tuning. At NAACL.

He et al., 2024. Data Poisoning for In-context Learning. At ICML.

**W5 & Q: The analysis assumes that “examples close to the query” are beneficial ... How would the gating mechanism behave if the nearest examples to the query are misleading or adversarially labeled? Does the exponential decay still guarantee robustness, or could it amplify incorrect patterns?**

**A5**: This is a great question. We thank the reviewer for the stimulating perspective. We would like to clarify that the gating mechanism still guarantees robustness if the nearest examples to the query are misleading or adversarially labeled. Thus, our analysis does NOT assume examples close to the query are beneficial. From (i) of Corollary 2, we show that the gating values on examples with outliers are close to 0, which indicates that the nonlinear gating filters out examples containing additive outliers rather than incorporates the effect of these examples in the prediction, even if these examples are close to the query. This is also empirically verified by Figure 4. Figure 4 shows that the gating values on examples with outliers are tiny, no matter where they are located, while the gating values are large and exhibit an exponential decay only on examples without outliers as the distance from the query increases.

summary.value: This paper focuses on building theoretical understanding of the Mamba model for its powerful in-context learning capability. According to the results, the authors demonstrate that Mamba leverages the linear attention layer to select informative context examples and uses the nonlinear gating layers to suppress the influence of outliers.

strengths.value:
- This paper is the first paper to theoretically understand the in-context capability of Mamba, which is an essential contribution.
- The paper is well written. 
- The empirical results are good.

weaknesses.value:
- The paper mainly focuses on the one-layer Mamba model, which cannot be seen as a comprehensive understanding of Mamba. However, this is not a significant drawback due to the complex large models.
- As a following question, can a model with just one layer achieve the similar capability of large Mamba models, such as in-context learning?
- The assumptions, which decompose the data into components of relevant and irrelevant parts, in Section 3.2 are interesting. I think such assumptions contribute to the theoretical analyses later. However, I am curious about whether such assumptions work in practice. In other words, can you provide some empirical or simple theoretical results to demonstrate that some assumptions are derived from the real cases?
- In Remark 4, a comparison between Mamba and the linear Transformer is reported. Specifically, compared to Mamba, the linear Transformer should satisfy some specific conditions for similar performance as Mamba. This is interesting. However, is there any empirical evidence to support the summaries? For example, consider two LLMs with the same architecture and trained with different hyperparameters. Do the empirical evaluations support your theoretical results?

comment.value:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable evaluation and suggestions.

**W1 & W2: The paper mainly focuses on the one-layer Mamba model, which cannot be seen as a comprehensive understanding of Mamba. However, this is not a significant drawback due to the complex large models. As a following question, can a model with just one layer achieve the similar capability of large Mamba models, such as in-context learning?**

**A1**: This is a great question! We explain the reason why we study one-layer Mamba as follows. First, for the optimization and generalization analysis of the related architecture, Transformers, the state-of-the-art theoretical works [Huang et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a;2025] recently published at top ML conferences like ICLR, Neurips, and ICML also focus on one-layer models only.  That is because the loss landscape for multi-layer neural networks, not just Mamba, is highly nonlinear and non-convex due to the interactions between multiple nonlinear functions. The extension to multi-layer neural networks requires a more complicated characterization of the gradient updates. 

Second,  to the best of our knowledge, no existing works theoretically study the generalization and the mechanism of Mamba, even for the one-layer case. Note that the learning problem of the one-layer Mamba is already highly nonlinear and nonconvex. The simplification of one-layer Mamba enables us to make contributions under our theoretical settings. Our work is the first to prove the ICL generalization ability of Mamba. Our analysis provides a comparison with Transformers in terms of robustness. The simplification also enables us to characterize the effect of different components of Mamba models, including the attention and nonlinear gating layer, in the learning process. 


Third, the theoretical conclusions of one-layer Mamba are empirically verified by multi-layer models to some extent. We justify our theoretical findings on the three-layer Mamba in Section 4.2. Figures 2 and 3 show the results of the first Mamba layer to verify the ICL mechanism characterized in Corollaries 1 and 2. The results of the other two layers can be found in Figures 4 and 5 in Appendix A. This implies that our generalization results of Mamba can potentially be extended to multi-layer cases. We leave the detailed theoretical analysis of the extension as future work.

For your follow-up question in Weakness 2, a one-layer model is worse than large mamba models in learning complex tasks in context due to a lack of expressive power. A one-layer Mamba or SSM-like model has so far only been theoretically proven to handle simple tasks, such as in-context linear regression [Li et al., 2024b; Jiang et al., 2025]. Unlike these works, our study analyzes Mamba’s ICL capabilities on classification problems in the presence of outliers. We believe our results lay the foundation for future theoretical studies of deep Mamba models on more complex tasks.

Huang et al., 2024. In-context convergence of transformers. At ICML.

Li et al., 2024a. How Do Nonlinear Transformers Learn and Generalize in In-Context Learning? At ICML.

Jiang et al., 2024. Unveil Benign Overfitting for Transformer in Vision: Training Dynamics, Convergence, and Generalization. At Neurips.

Li et al., 2025. Training Nonlinear Transformers for Chain-of-Thought Inference: A Theoretical Generalization Analysis. At ICLR.

Jiang et al., 2025. Trained Mamba Emulates Online Gradient Descent in In-Context Linear Regression. At Neurips.

Li et al., 2024b. Fine-grained Analysis of In-context Linear Estimation: Data, Architecture, and Beyond. At Neurips.

Specifically, the formulation of relevant patterns that determine labels is inspired by the observation that real-world data often admits a sparse representation [Wright et al., 2010], i.e., the data can be expressed using a set of low-dimensional and sparse patterns that form a dictionary, and the associated labels are functions of these underlying representations. Irrelevant patterns refer to additional information in the data that is unrelated to the classification task, e.g., backgrounds in images or unimportant words in language. Learning deep neural network features using a sparse representation formulation has been shown to be highly effective by strong empirical performance in diverse tasks such as face recognition and image denoising [Wright et al., 2010]. This indicates that sparse representation aligns well with the underlying structure of real-world data. Moreover, some existing empirical works [Engler et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024] demonstrate that embeddings of real-world data between semantically different data are discriminative, which is also aligned with our data formulation based on relevant and irrelevant patterns. 

We also conduct an experiment to validate our data formulation with a real-world setting. The dataset we use is the sentiment classification dataset SST-2.  We conduct Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on sentence vectors of different classes obtained by DistillBert. Then the classification task is performed on the data that only keeps a few PCA components. The following table shows that when keeping the top few principal components, i.e., 10 out of 768 in total, the classification performance using these principal components is already close to the baseline using original data. This indicates that real-world data can be represented as a linear combination of orthogonal vectors, where these principal components exactly correspond to the relevant patterns we formulate.

**W4: In Remark 4, a comparison between Mamba and the linear Transformer is reported... However, is there any empirical evidence to support the summaries? For example, consider two LLMs with the same architecture and trained with different hyperparameters. Do the empirical evaluations support your theoretical results?**

**A3**: The conclusions in Remarks 4 and 5 show that, to achieve comparable performance, the linear attention requires weaker conditions during training, while the additional stronger condition required for linear attention appears only in Remark 5, i.e., that during testing, $\alpha$, the fraction of outliers, must not exceed $1/2$. Mamba does not require this condition. This is because our theory shows that the effect of Mamba’s nonlinear gating is to remove outliers (Corollary 2), allowing Mamba models to tolerate a high outlier fraction. In contrast, the linear Transformer cannot learn the outlier at all, and therefore needs the outlier fraction to be the minority to ensure correct final predictions.

This insight is supported by real-world experiments. In vision tasks, Mamba and other SSM models have been shown to exhibit stronger robustness than Transformer architectures against outliers such as adversarial attacks and common corruptions [Park et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Malik et al., 2025]. In particular, [Du et al., 2024] finds that the parameter $\Delta$ are key to Mamba’s defense capability under white-box attacks. Since in our setting $\Delta$ are formulated as functions of the nonlinear gating parameters $w$ (line 135), this observation is consistent with our theoretical conclusion in Corollary 2, i.e., nonlinear gating removes outliers and thereby improves robustness.

Because Mamba-based LLM are still under development, comparisons between the two types of LLMs on robustness are still less explored. However, the empirical findings mentioned above can provide experimental support for our theoretical results to some extent.

summary.value: This paper shows a one-layer Mamba block can implement in-context learning (ICL) on stylized binary tasks, and its nonlinear gate is the key: linear attention selects helpful examples; the gate suppresses outliers and induces a local bias. Compared to a linear-attention Transformer (same setting), Mamba may train a bit slower but stays accurate under a much higher fraction of corrupted examples—even approaching 100% under their assumptions.

strengths.value:
- The theoretical claims seem to align with empirical evidence (on the high level), e.g., the paper’s core takeaway—Mamba’s gate makes ICL more robust to corrupted prompts than a pure linear-attention Transformer—is directionally consistent with what the community has observed.

- Clear mechanistic story: linear attention aligns to the query’s relevant pattern; gating both suppresses outliers and biases to nearby positions.

weaknesses.value:
1. The paper studies a stylized binary, pattern-based ICL task where each input contains exactly one relevant and one irrelevant orthogonal pattern of equal norm; labels depend only on the relevant pattern. This is a clean but **unnatural** abstraction for real data. Results derived on this task may not transfer to more general tasks studies in practice. 

2. Outlier modeling is also narrow/artificial: Outliers are injected additively, orthogonal to both relevant and irrelevant patterns during training, and at test time are linear combinations of the training-time outlier directions with a positivity constraint.

3. Transformer comparator is a very specific “linear attention” variant (no softmax, multi-heads...). So the headline advantage (“Mamba tolerates higher outlier fractions”) is established against a simplified comparator that may be unrepresentative of modern Transformers. This undermines the breadth of the claim.

questions.value:
1. The test outlier is a positive combination of train outliers (Condition (11)). How realistic is this in language tasks? What happens for combinations with mixed signs or novel directions?

2. Can you extend beyond binary classification to multiclass or regression within the same framework? Where do the proofs fail?

We thank the reviewer for the valuable evaluation and suggestions. 

**W1: The paper studies a stylized binary ... This is a clean but unnatural abstraction for real data. Results derived on this task may not transfer to more general tasks studies in practice.**

**A1**: This is a great question. First, the data formulation of relevant and irrelevant patterns that are orthogonal is inspired by the latent sparse representation of real-world data [Wright et al., 2010]. Specifically, the formulation of relevant patterns that determine labels is inspired by the observation that real-world data often admits a sparse representation [Wright et al., 2010], i.e., the data can be expressed using a set of low-dimensional and sparse patterns that form a dictionary, and the associated labels are functions of these underlying representations. Irrelevant patterns refer to additional information in the data that is unrelated to the classification task, e.g., backgrounds in images or unimportant words in language. Learning deep neural network features using a sparse representation formulation has been shown to be highly effective by strong empirical performance in diverse tasks such as face recognition and image denoising [Wright et al., 2010]. This indicates that sparse representation aligns well with the underlying structure of real-world data. Moreover, some existing empirical works [Engler et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024] demonstrate that embeddings of real-world data between semantically different data are discriminative, which is also aligned with our data formulation based on relevant and irrelevant patterns. 

Second, we would like to clarify that this paper is in fact built upon MILDER assumptions compared with existing theoretical works. The orthogonality decomposition on patterns is a common practice in prior theoretical works [Allen-Zhu & Li, 2023; Huang et al., 2024], which especially assume different data to be orthogonal to each other. This assumption highlights the distinction between patterns with different semantics in a concise way and simplifies factors that are irrelevant to the analysis. Since we decompose the data into sums of relevant and irrelevant patterns, we in fact do not require different data embeddings to be mutually orthogonal. 

To address your concerns, we conduct two experiments to validate our data formulation and conclusion with a real-world setting. The dataset we use is the sentiment classification dataset SST-2.  We conduct Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on sentence vectors of different classes obtained by DistillBert. Then the classification task is performed on the data that only keeps a few PCA components. The following table shows that when keeping the top few principal components, i.e., 10 out of 768 in total, the classification performance using these principal components is already close to the baseline using original data. This indicates that real-world data can be represented as a linear combination of orthogonal vectors, where these principal components exactly correspond to relevant patterns we formulate. 

|# of principal components | 5            | 7          | 10         |  768 (Baseline)|
|------------|------|-------|-----|------|
| Accuracy                            |74.08% |76.72% |78.90% |80.05%            |

We then conduct an ICL experiment by constructing each prompt with 8 examples and one query. The outlier phrase “James Bond” is inserted into a randomly selected example at a random position. The training outlier fraction $p\_a=0.25$. All models are constrained to have 3 layers and 2 heads. The table below compares Mamba and the linear Transformer under the testing outlier fraction $\alpha=0.75$ across the three outlier placements. Recall that FQ, R, CQ represent three kinds of outlier placements, i.e, “farthest from the query”, “random positions”, and “closest to the query”, respectively. The results show that Mamba performs better overall than the linear Transformer, and its performance at the CQ position is the lowest compared to FQ and R. This is consistent with the synthetic experiments in Table 1 of our paper and validates our analysis in Corollary 2 regarding the mechanism of nonlinear gating. We have included these results in Appendix B.2 of the updated paper.

|---|---|---|
|FQ | 74.10% |70.18%|
|R |73.86%| 69.98% |
|CQ | 72.45%|  69.82%|

comment.value:
**W2 & Q1: Outlier modeling is also narrow/artificial ... How realistic is this in language tasks? What happens for combinations with mixed signs or novel directions?**

**A2**: The notion of additive and orthogonal outliers can characterize data poisoning attacks, where the predicted label of a context example can be changed by inserting specific phrases into the context input.  Specifically, as illustrated in Example 1 of our paper,  an outlier is a phrase inserted into the sentence. Then, it can be modeled as a new embedding added to the sentence embedding. Because such inserted phrases are typically unrelated to the task-specific keywords, for example, in Example 1, “James Bond” is unrelated to the keywords of sentiment classification, then this additive embedding makes the outlier orthogonal to the relevant patterns. We believe this is a mild assumption that characterizes the data poisoning attacks. A similar assumption is also made in [Li et al., 2025] for robustness analysis of Transformers in ICL.

We would like to clarify that test outliers allow mixed signs. Equation 11 indicates that the summation of the linear coefficients, rather than each linear coefficient, shall be positive. If the summation of linear coefficients $L$ is negative, the testing outlier will be in the opposite direction of the main features of the trained $w$. Therefore, $G_{i,l+1}(w)$ will not be activated due to the sigmoid term $\sigma(w^\top p_i)$  in Equation 3. If there is a novel direction in the testing outlier that is orthogonal to all the training outliers and relevant and irrelevant patterns, then such a direction does not affect the gating mechanism in detecting outliers. Therefore, we allow such a component to be added in Equation 11 without affecting our conclusion. Specifically, the condition becomes $$V'=\\{v |v=\sum\_{i=1}\^V \lambda_i v_i\^*+u, \sum\_{i=1}\^V\lambda\_i\geq L>0, u\perp \\{ v_r^\*\\}\_{r=1}\^V\cup\\{ \mu_j^\*\\}\_{j=1}\^{M_1}\cup\\{ \nu_k^\*\\}\_{k=1}\^{M_2}\\}.$$

We have made revisions accordingly in the updated version. We thank the reviewer for this valuable question. 

Li et al., 2025. On the Robustness of Transformers against Context Hijacking for Linear Classification. At Neurips.

**W3: Transformer comparator is a very specific “linear attention” variant. So the headline advantage is established against a simplified comparator that may be unrepresentative of modern Transformers. This undermines the breadth of the claim.**

**A3**: Thank you for the question. We agree that we should clearly state in the paper that the robustness advantages of Mamba are compared against the linear Transformer. We have already added “one-layer” in P2 of Section 3.1 and the title of Section 3.4 to avoid confusion. We explain why the main comparison in the paper is with the linear Transformer as follows.
First, since Mamba can be viewed as a linear attention layer plus a nonlinear gating layer, the comparison between Mamba and a linear Transformer enables the characterization of the impact of the nonlinear gating layer. Specifically, this analysis allows us to attribute the observed differences in robustness, i.e., one-layer single-head Mamba can tolerate an outlier fraction that is larger than what one-layer single-head linear Transformers can, to the mechanism of the nonlinear gating layer. Our mechanism analysis in Corollary 2 also justifies that the nonlinear gating layer selectively removing outlier-containing context examples indeed makes Mamba robust to a high outlier fraction.

Second, if we compare Mamba with a nonlinear Transformer, we cannot theoretically justify the effects of different components in Mamba. Such a comparison will involve comparing a linear attention + nonlinear gating architecture to a nonlinear attention model, which introduces a confounding factor in the analysis. 
However, we believe that nonlinear attention plays a significant role in enhancing the generalization and robustness of the model, and we conduct experiments using softmax attention as a comparison with Mamba and linear attention models. We repeat the experiment in Table 1 using a three-layer single-head softmax Transformer with $\alpha=0.5$. $d=72$. The result shows that the performance of softmax attention is better than linear attention and close to Mamba. Meanwhile, there is no significant accuracy drop in the CQ setting for softmax attention. This is because Mamba is more vulnerable than the softmax Transformer to outliers that appear near the query without robust training [Wang et al., 2024]. 

We have incorporated the above discussion in the updated version. We thank the reviewer for raising this valuable point for discussion.


| | Softmax Transformer |LT| Mamba|
|---|---|---|---|
|FQ|99.40% | 93.68% |99.73%|
|R|99.26%|94.12%|99.67%|
|CQ|99.38%|93.96%|82.73%|


Wang et al., 2024. Understanding and Mitigating Bottlenecks of State Space Models through the Lens of Recency and Over-smoothing

**Q2: Can you extend beyond binary classification to multiclass or regression within the same framework? Where do the proofs fail?**

**A4**: This is an interesting question. Our analytical framework can indeed be applied to multi-classification problems and linear regression problems. We retain only the discussion of the binary classification case in the main text to highlight the main contributions of our theoretical analysis.

We first provide a brief overview of a straightforward extension for multi-classification in the updated Appendix E.7. The basic idea is that we consider a $C=2^H$-classification problem, which can be decomposed into $H$ independent binary classification problems. Then, each label becomes $H$-dimensional. Each input is reconstructed as a concatenation of $H$ binary inputs formulated in Equation 6. The prompt is defined as $P=(P_1^\top, P_2^\top,\cdots, P_H^\top)^\top$, where $$P_h=\begin{pmatrix}
    x_{1,h} & x_{2,h} &\cdots & x_{l,h} & x_{query,h}\\\\
    y_{1,h} & y_{2,h} &\cdots & y_{l,h} & 0
    \end{pmatrix}\in R^{(d+1)\times(l+1)}.$$

Then, we can consider an $H$-head Mamba model parameterized by $\Psi=\\{\\{W\_{B,h}, W\_{C,h}, w\_h\\}\_{h=1}\^H\\}$. Following Equation 3, the output of one-layer Mamba can be rewritten as $
F(\Psi; P)=(F_1(\Psi; P), F_2(\Psi; P),\cdots, F_H(\Psi; P))^\top$, where  $F_h(\Psi; P)=\sum_{i=1}\^{l+1} G_{i,l+1}(w\_h) y\_{i,h} p_{i.h}\^\top W\_{B,h}^\top W\_{C,h} p\_{query,h}$. 

Our analytical technique and results for the binary classification case can then be applied to this multi-classification problem. 

Our analysis of Mamba can similarly be extended to the linear regression setting. We provide a brief discussion in the updated Appendix E.8. Our theoretical analysis can be extended to linear regression problems. Note that [Huang et al., 2024] analyze the linear regression problem in the ICL framework for one-layer single-head Transformers under similar data assumptions to ours, i.e., that the data are defined by orthogonal relevant features. For Mamba, we can conduct a similar analysis. The main challenges lie in the gradient and convergence analysis under the squared loss, as well as in the formulation and analysis of outliers. One option is to formulate the context label with outliers as random outputs. With squared loss, the gradient of $W_C$, $W_B$, and $w$ are computed as
   $$ \frac{\partial\ell(\Psi; P^n,z^n)}{\partial W_C} = (F(\Psi, P)-z^n) \sum_{i=1}^{l} G^n\_{i,l+1}(w) y_i^n W_B p_i^n { p_{query}^n}^\top,$$
    $$\frac{\partial\ell(\Psi; P^n,z^n)}{\partial W_B} = (F(\Psi, P)-z^n) \sum_{i=1}^{l+1} G^n_{i,l+1}(w) y_i W_C p_{query} p_{i}^\top,$$
$$\frac{\partial \ell(\Psi; P^n, z^n)}{\partial w}\\
    =(F(\Psi, P)-z^n) \sum_{i=1}^{l} y_i^n {p_i^n}^\top W_B^\top W_C p_{query}^n G^n_{i,l+1}(w)(\sum_{s=i+1}^{l+1} \sigma(w^\top p_s^n)p_s^n-(1-\sigma(w^\top p_i^n)) p_i^n).$$

Since $F(\Psi, P)$ is generally between $-1$ and $1$ before convergence, we can still ensure that the model can learn relevant patterns by gradient updates, which is consistent with the case of classification problem. Random labels for outlier examples cancel out their gradient contribution, leading the nonlinear gating to learn outlier patterns. Then, the further analysis is almost the same as the classification problem.



Huang et al., 2024. In-context convergence of transformers. At ICML.

Dear AC/SAC/PC,

We first want to thank you for handling our paper.

We would like to briefly summarize and emphasize how we addressed the reviewers’ concerns and updated our paper accordingly during the Author-Reviewer discussion phase. Our initial overall scores were 6, 6, 4, 4. In particular, the reviewers with a score of 4 are Reviewers okLR and v2NB. The main issues raised by the reviewers were as follows:
* **Q1** raised by Reviewers okLR (score 4),1e2F (score 6), and v2NB (score 4): Our theoretical analysis was based on simplified data and task formulation, and the paper lacks experiments on real datasets as well as empirical validation of our assumptions.
* **Q2** raised by Reviewers okLR (score 4) and 2qkh (score 6): Our theoretical discussion of Transformers only involves the linear attention model rather than general Transformer architectures.
* **Q3** raised by Reviewers v2NB (score 4) and 2qkh (score 6): Our analysis of Mamba’s mechanism shows that examples close to the query have a large impact on the final prediction. If these near-query examples contain outliers, will they negatively affect the prediction? 
* **Q4** raised by Reviewer okLR (score 4): Can the analysis be extended to multiclass or regression?

Regarding **Q1**, we explained that **the assumptions we use are motivated by the sparse representation perspective of data modeling**. By comparing with prior theoretical works, we showed that our assumptions are in fact **milder** than those commonly adopted in the literature. It is worth noting that Reviewer 1e2F (score 6) also thinks our assumptions "**contribute to the theoretical analyses**" and the simplification "**is not a significant drawback**". In addition, we conducted experiments on a real-world sentiment-classification dataset to provide empirical validation. These experiments demonstrated that 
* Real data can indeed be decomposed into a small number of approximately orthogonal principal components, without degrading model performance, which is consistent with our assumption.
* On real-world data, the performance comparison between Mamba and linear attention matches the behavior observed in our synthetic experiments, aligning with our theoretical predictions.
For the detailed response, please refer to [Response to Reviewer okLR Part I](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tswBfpkwHn&noteId=tmZbudbkot). We have included these experiments in Appendix B.2.

Regarding **Q2**, we explained that the comparison between the one-layer Mamba and the linear-attention model is designed to **isolate the effect of the nonlinear gating mechanism**, since Mamba can be decomposed into "linear attention + nonlinear gating." In addition, we conducted experiments with **softmax Transformers** and **multi-head attention**. The results show that Softmax attention performs better than linear attention and is close to Mamba, indicating that the nonlinearity of softmax improves robustness in the setting studied in our paper. Meanwhile, increasing the number of heads provides almost no benefit, showing that multi-head attention is not particularly helpful for the non-causal task structure we study. For the detailed response, please refer to [Response to Reviewer okLR Part II](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tswBfpkwHn&noteId=WVd4nwvo33) and [Response to Reviewer 2qkh Part I](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tswBfpkwHn&noteId=6YLO3Fuwsi). We have included the related discussion in Remark 6 and Appendix B.1. 

Regarding **Q3**, we both theoretically and empirically clarified that Mamba’s final prediction depends on **outlier-free examples** that are close to the query, rather than on all examples that are close to the query. Robustness training effectively guides Mamba to learn the outlier feature, which in turn activates the model’s ability to resist outliers. For the detailed response, please refer to [Response to Reviewer v2NB Part II](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tswBfpkwHn&noteId=HVa915qfNa) and [Response to Reviewer 2qkh Part I](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tswBfpkwHn&noteId=6YLO3Fuwsi).

Regarding **Q4**, we showed that our analytical framework can be extended to both **multi-class classification** and **linear regression** problems. We provided preliminary derivations in the Appendices E.7 and E.8. For the response, please refer to [Response to Reviewer okLR Part III](https://openreview.net/forum?id=tswBfpkwHn&noteId=cBhrb807Eh).

Our theoretical investigation of Mamba’s mechanisms in ICL has been recognized as a **"solid" (Reviewer 2qkh), "novel, nontrivial" (Reviewer v2NB), and "essential contribution" (Reviewer 1e2F), which is aligned with empirical evidence (Reviewer okLR)**. We would be deeply grateful if you could take the above points into consideration when making your final decision. Thank you!

Authors
